# Adding Predictors

Up to now every model has had exactly one predictor. That was a teaching convenience, not a research design. Almost nothing you care about has one cause, and almost no variable you measure is unentangled from the rest.

This week we put two predictors in the same model, and the whole week turns on one phrase: **holding the other predictor constant**. It is not a hedge and it is not boilerplate. It changes what the coefficient is a number *about* — from "the difference between people who differ in X" to "the difference between people who differ in X and are otherwise matched on everything else in the model."

::: callout-note
## The sentence to watch for this week

A slope is not a property of a variable. It is a property of a **variable inside a particular model**. Change what else is in the model and the number changes — sometimes a little, sometimes a lot, occasionally all the way to the opposite sign.
:::

We open with a county fire department, 300 fires, and a regression that says sending more fire trucks causes more damage. The output is correct. The conclusion is lethal. Fixing it takes exactly one more variable.

Then we do it with real survey data, where the honest finding is less dramatic: two predictors that barely move each other, which turns out to be the common case and a perfectly reportable result.

::: callout-important
## This is the week the midterm needs

Part 6 of the [Midterm Project](../labs/midterm-project.html) asks for a two-predictor model, each coefficient interpreted with its *holding constant* clause, and a model-comparison table with ΔR². All of that is today.

If you have been waiting on Part 6, you are no longer waiting. **The project is due Tuesday 10/27.**
:::
